segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: What's going on here, Jacques? Clearly someone — if it's Joe McMoneagle, let's just call them Gilbert — someone invited Gilbert to a secure facility, presumably a secure government facility. Yet at the same time we have the government, in the form of AARO, the Pentagon, asserting blue and blind that there is absolutely no evidence of extraterrestrial non-human intelligence engagement with this planet. We know that's not true. What's going on, sir? You probably more than anyone know the answer to that question.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: It's a central question, of course, and I don't want to treat it in a humorous way, but I recall a conversation with Dr. Josef Allen Hynek when I was working with him back at Northwestern. I said: what does the Air Force say, what does the Air Force think? And he sat me down and he said: Jacques, you have to understand there is no such thing as the US Air Force. There are projects within the Air Force that do different things, and that's legitimate. They're looking at different parts of the whole planet with the tools they have, and they have different opinions about things, and they have budgets to pursue different things with different projects, and many times they don't know about the other project.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I wasn't part of the UFO hearings, but back in the late 1980s I was part of a study of emergency management and how computers could be used for emergency management in the United States. We were told that there were only two of us who were not cleared for anything at the time, working in industry, and all the others were from different agencies. This was organized by Congress, by Al Gore, and this happened on two successive years. I had three occasions to be part of congressional hearings on emergency management, and these were two of them. It was fascinating, because two of the people there are people I respect more than anybody else in the world: Mr. Tom Belden, who was with the IDA, and Arthur C. Lundahl, who was head of the photographic agency that has now been absorbed into other agencies, and was responsible for the photographic intelligence around the world. He broke the story of what the U-2s were doing, he also broke the story of the rockets in Cuba, and we became friends. These two men sort of took me under their wing as a result of these hearings in Congress. My testimony there has been published and it's black and white: this is Tuesday, October 9, 1984, Information technology for emergency management. We are in a similar situation now, and yes, we can disclose, but the structure is complex.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: Tom Belden told me that as part of his career he had been in charge of studying crises. He had reported to the president on the five major crises over several presidential periods, including the Cuban crisis. And he told me that he had been in charge at one time of getting together all the people who would be involved if there was a nuclear attack on the United States. He said he got all the clearances, because he was in the right place to do it. There were 54 projects that would be operating if there was a notice of an incoming nuclear missile from Russia. So he got clearances for all the projects and he called people to a room for a meeting. He said the first 10 minutes were amazing, because half of them did not know the other half — they did not know the existence of the other half. And there were people there in blue jeans, and some general would say: well, who are you, why are you here? And the guy would say: well, I'm with <abbr title="American Telephone and Telegraph">AT&T</abbr>, sir, and when you push the button on your red phone, if I'm not there that red phone isn't going to work, because you're in Kansas and I'm in Boulder, inside a mountain, and I see when you push the button, then I have to push my button. And they had no idea. He said it was amazing, the first 10 minutes were really the key to the entire awakening that we wouldn't know what to do if there was an incoming missile. Unfortunately, I think time has passed and I assume we're better prepared.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: But the situation with UFOs is the same. UFOs manifest in the water, as you know, they manifest in the air. They may be tracked, the way Dr. Avi Loeb wants to do it at Harvard. In my cases they are not tracked: they appear out of nowhere, in the field. And I'm continuing to publish those cases, because people don't know them. People assume they come and they can be tracked. Some of them can, not all of them.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Just to echo what you say there about how it continues on, the same problem of compartmentalization continues in the UFO field. In your book Forbidden Science 7 you talk about how Dr. Eric Davis probably knows more about the real legacy program than Dr. Sean Kirkpatrick, who was running the AARO program inside the Pentagon. You can see the probability that the people charged with investigating UAPs inside the Pentagon probably know less than someone on the outside.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I think the disclosure that we need is that there is a real problem, that we don't know what those things are, and that they are just as real as this computer in front of me. Now, beyond that, the disclosure would be that we don't have any idea what their goal is, what their structure is, or where they come from. Everybody has been assuming they must come from another planet like ours. If you talk to an astronomer, he'll say: you're free to believe whatever you want, but that's not the way the universe works.
